[WP] A group of theologians capture a great demon and ask him what?

"so, say the chant, sprinkle the spices and then its contained" Mary asked tentatively to adicous. adicous was a trader by day, not a headline-reaching one but one who had strung himself to, and been strung between, some of the most important merchant connections in the region. his office had only one small tiny window, but he had feasted with the emperor on occasion.

he also had, unseemly, connections to the occult world, so the rumors said. but David and Mary were beyond the rumors now. they were sitting in front of the proof. jovially, adicous leaned forward toward the two, "yes, and i know your first demon is a scary prospect, but believe me, there business minded people with slightly more blood-rage. youve already paid quite a price and we've known each other for years. its all square right now". he patted an envelope in his coat pocket, and snapped the buttons closed, sealing that envelope from all records and further mention. david cringed at what the price had been, and only Mary's clever covering had prevented them both from being booted from the society.

he cringed a bit more, then, remembering what had necessitated the exchange. the pair should have been a lot more careful when dabbling in blood magic, but the society's taboo made it too tempting to ignore. David nodded to adicous, unsure of what could be added to the discussion, he grabbed the vial from the desk, and they stepped out silently.

in the night, later, when a quarter of a bottle of wine was shared between mary and david to loosen their fear, they followed the instructions. a bonfire in a remote hovel. spices, a dark chanting that was best glossed over. a dead animal sacrifice seeding the bonfire for attraction. and then, the demon.

it, was ten feet tall. it was reddish and glowing like coals, it said "you have summoned me, make it quick". the pair looked at each other, then the demon. David pulled a tarp off the body of their former head decon, who had had the misfortune to stumble on a blood-spell at the wrong precise moment, he said, "we need the essence of a soul to, conveniently disappear".

Actually, he is not incorrect. The article is just written very poorly.

Here are two quotes from the article:

"BioCarbon Engineering wants to use drones for good, using the technology to seed up to one billion trees a year, all without having to set foot on the ground."

"With two operators manning multiple drones, he thinks it should be possible to plant up to 36,000 trees a day, and at around 15% of the cost of traditional methods."

Lauren Fletcher never made these statements himself. They are extrapolations from the article, and the pieces of information are not directly connected. One is a long-term goal, while one is a short-term goal.

They're trying to do something good here, but I'm pretty skeptical. Split some areas into control blocks, plant one half traditionally, the other from the air and come back in a couple years. I really doubt his method will yield acceptable results. The number of plants you need to air drop versus the number required if you plant on the ground will be significant. The ones that "take" when air-dropped are likely to be in bunches. I don't have numbers on viability but I know airdrop has been tried already and that we still use human planters on the ground in North America. I doubt this expense is endured for altruistic reasons.

Rachel Bryk, one of the developers for Dolphin (Gamecube / Wii emulator), passed away at only 23 years old.
Just found out that she committed suicide. Not sure about the reliability, but according to this article it's because of online harassment from 4chan.

Harassment from 4chan may have been a part of it, but it is not the main component. She probably already had depression, and when you're in that state of mind, almost anything can push you over the edge. A normal, healthy person would just shrug it off. I mean really, who gives a fuck about the opinions of a bunch of online twats?

So, I think it's kind of a bad idea that when people commit suicide we focus on the external factors. This kind of brushes aside the more important issue of mental health in general, and things like depression, which is the real cause. Obviously, people have been through a lot more harrowing things than this, but have not taken their lives. The battle that Rachel Bryk had was an internal one.

I'm just saying this from experience.

Definitely shitty of people to do that to her. I'm sure it's a great loss to the community.

 

However, it sounds like she had some mental illness that required treatment. Mentally healthy individuals don't typically take their own lives because of "cyberbullying." Lets not blame faceless individuals for this tragedy.
